---
title: Command Line Interface (CLI)
---

The `sib` command creates keys, enrolls them, signs instructions, verifies files and decodes
blocks. With a dev key it runs in dev mode and every command that signs or verifies prints the
dev-mode warning to standard error; with a passkey enrolled it signs through the browser and
verifies in enforced mode.

All commands read `SIB_HOME` for the directory that holds keys and the registry (default:
`~/.sib`).

Inside the repository, run it as `uv run sib`. After `source .venv/bin/activate`, or after
`uv tool install --editable .`, plain `sib` works; the examples below use the plain form.


## Basic Usage

```bash
# Create a dev key and enroll it for a signer
sib keygen --signer alice@example.com --enroll

# Or enroll a passkey (Touch ID, Windows Hello, a security key) through the browser
sib enroll --signer alice@example.com

# Sign an instruction, appending the block to the nearest AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md
sib sign "You may deploy the current main branch to staging whenever the test suite passes."

# Or name the signer, the context and an expiry, and write the block elsewhere
sib sign --signer alice@example.com --expires 2h --audience acme/dev-agent --out block.txt \
  "You may deploy the current main branch to staging whenever the test suite passes."

# Sign the contents of a file, or anything on standard input
sib sign --file instruction.txt
git log -1 --format=%s | sib sign

# Verify every block in a file for a given audience
sib verify CLAUDE.md --audience acme/dev-agent

# Decode blocks without verifying them
sib inspect CLAUDE.md
```


## Commands

### keygen

Create a dev-mode Ed25519 key under `$SIB_HOME/dev-keys/` and optionally enroll it. Give
`--signer`, `--kid`, or both.

`--signer ID`
: The signer the key belongs to. When `--kid` is omitted the key identifier is derived as
  `<signer>#dev-<year>-<month>` (e.g., `alice@example.com#dev-2026-09`).

`--kid ID`
: Key identifier, by convention `signer#label`. Overrides the derived name.

`--enroll`
: Also add the public key to the registry. Requires `--signer`. Refused when that signer already
  holds a passkey: a software key signs from a file with nobody present, and anything that can run
  `sib` can create one, so a second weaker key under a name that already has a passkey can only
  weaken what a signature from that person means. Without `--enroll` the key file is still
  written, because a key nobody is enrolled for confers nothing.

`--audience ID`
: Record this as the registry's `default_audience`, so `sign`, `verify` and `install` need no
  audience afterwards. See [audience](#audience) for what the name should be.

`--dev`
: Accepted for clarity; dev mode is the only mode `keygen` supports.

### enroll

Enroll a passkey through the browser, or add a public key given on the command line. Without
`--public-key` the command starts the local signing app, opens the enroll page and waits for the
authenticator; see [Biometric Signing](../components/signing.qmd#enrollment).

`--signer ID`
: The signer the key belongs to. Required.

`--kid ID`
: Key identifier. Derived as `<signer>#passkey-<id>` for a passkey; required with
  `--public-key`.

`--public-key B64URL`
: Enroll this raw public key, base64url encoded, instead of a passkey.

`--alg ALG`
: Signature algorithm of `--public-key` (default: `EdDSA`).

`--dev`
: Mark the key as a dev-mode key. Without it the key is enrolled as `enforced`.

`--timeout SECONDS`
: How long to wait for the browser (default: 180).

`--no-browser`
: Print the page URL instead of opening a browser.

`--browser NAME`
: The browser to open the page in, when the system default lacks passkey support or a password
  manager in it captures the prompt: a name the Python `webbrowser` module knows (`safari`,
  `chrome`, `firefox`) or a command the URL is appended to (`'open -a Safari'`). Defaults to
  `SIB_BROWSER`, then the system default.

### sign

Clearsign an instruction. The command prints the canonical text, the terms and the destination
before signing, so what you see is what you sign. With a passkey it opens the sign page and waits
for the authenticator; with a dev key it signs at once.

The instruction itself is the one positional argument, so the short form is the whole command:

```bash
sib sign "You may deploy the current main branch to staging."
```

Given no argument and neither `--text` nor `--file`, the instruction is read from standard input.
At a terminal, where that would hang with no prompt, the command says what to type instead.

Before anything is signed the command prints every term that carries authority — the canonical
text, the signer, the key, the authorization context, the expiry and the file the block will go
into — and asks for a yes. The question is read from `/dev/tty` rather than standard input, so the
instruction can arrive on a pipe while the answer still comes from the person at the keyboard. With
no terminal to ask at, the command refuses rather than assuming: `-y` is how an unattended signer
says so.

With a passkey, the terms include a six-digit confirmation code, and the sign page shows the same
code. See [Confirmation code](../components/signing.qmd#confirmation-code) for why that matters.

Either identifier is enough: a `--kid` names its signer through the registry, and a `--signer`
with exactly one enrolled key names that key. A signer's passkeys are preferred over their dev
keys; with several candidates, the command lists them and asks for `--kid`. With neither, the
command signs as this machine's `git config user.email`, if a key is enrolled for it, and says
whom it chose — so the usual case needs no identifier at all. A git identity with no enrolled key
is an error rather than a guess, because guessing would surface later as `unknown_signer`, a long
way from the cause.

`--signer ID`
: The signer, written to the `iss` header field. Derived from `--kid` when omitted, then from
  `git config user.email`; checked for agreement when both it and `--kid` are given.

`--kid ID`
: The key to sign with. Derived from `--signer` when the signer has one candidate key.

`--expires DURATION`
: Validity window from now, as `30m`, `2h` or `1d`. Omitted by default, and a block with no `exp`
  does not expire: it is valid until it is removed from the file it lives in, which is what
  standing authorization in an instruction file is meant to be. An expiry is still the right choice
  for a block covering one task, and the only thing that limits a copy taken elsewhere.

`--audience ID`
: The authorization context the block is for. Falls back to `SIB_AUDIENCE` and then the registry's
  `default_audience`, and the signing preview names which source was used. Optional for a dev key;
  required for a passkey, because a block with no audience is refused in enforced mode.

`--canon RULE`
: Canonicalization rule (default: `text/1`). See [Canonicalization](../components/canonicalization.qmd).

`TEXT`
: The instruction, as a positional argument. Line structure does not matter under `text/1`.

`--text TEXT`
: The same thing as a flag, for a caller that would rather be explicit.

`--file PATH`
: File holding the instruction, or `-` for standard input.

`--out PATH`
: Write the block to this file, replacing what is there, or to standard output for `-`.

`--append PATH`
: Append the block to this file, rather than searching for one.

With neither flag the block is appended to the nearest instruction file: starting at the working
directory and walking up, the first `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` found, `AGENTS.md` winning within a
directory because that is the file Codex reads. The walk stops at the repository root, or at the
home directory outside a repository, so a block signed in one checkout cannot drift up into a file
that covers every checkout above it. With no such file anywhere on that path the block goes to
standard output; signing does not create an instruction file, because a block in a file nothing
reads authorizes nothing. Appending leaves a blank line before the block and never rewrites what
was already there.

`-y`, `--yes`
: Sign without confirming the terms first. For an unattended signer; it skips the one step that
  establishes a person approved these words.

`--dev`
: Sign with a dev key even when a passkey is enrolled; refuses a `--kid` that is not a dev key.

`--timeout SECONDS`, `--no-browser`, `--browser NAME`
: As for `enroll`.

### install

Install SIB into an agent harness. Takes the harness as a sub-subcommand.

#### install codex

Writes the auto-review configuration that makes Codex's reviewer run `sib verify` itself and score
a verified signature as user authorization. It is meant to be the only command you type before
launching Codex, so it asks for the two things no package can ship — a name for this authorization
context, and a key to sign with — rather than refusing until you have arranged them yourself.

It merges rather than overwrites, so it is safe to run against a configuration you already use.
Every setting it does not own is left where it is, the previous file is copied to
`<config>.sib-bak` before anything is written, and it asks before each change:

- **Naming this authorization context** — the context signed instructions are valid in. Asked
  first, with a suggestion built from the hostname and your account, such as
  `m4-watchtower/trevor-dev`. The answer is recorded as the registry's
  [`default_audience`](#audience), so `sign` and `verify` agree with the reviewer without being
  told. A vendor name is deliberately not suggested: `openai/codex` would be byte-identical in
  everyone's install and the check would stop distinguishing anything. Skipped when `--audience`,
  `SIB_AUDIENCE` or a recorded default already answers it.

- **Setting `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`** — the default is yes when the key is absent, and
  no when you have already set it to something else, since enabling the reviewer should not
  silently discard a choice you made. Declining still writes the policy; the reviewer can then be
  enabled per run with `codex exec --approve-for-me`.

- **Replacing `experimental_policy_template` or `extra_policy`** — asked only when a previous run
  (or you) already set them, and the default is no. Declining writes nothing at all.

- **Enrolling a signing key** — asked last, and only when no passkey is enrolled, which is exactly
  when the install cannot yet produce a signature that proves a person was there. With no keys at
  all, every block verifies as `unknown_signer`: the safe direction, and an inert one. With only
  software keys the install signs in dev mode, where a signature proves possession of a file and a
  block confers nothing as soon as any passkey exists — so an existing dev key is not a reason to
  stop asking. A passkey is the default, and the only offer once software keys exist; the signer
  defaults to the one already in the registry, or to this machine's `git config user.email`.

Writing the file is not among the questions: it is what the command does, `--print` is how you look
without writing, and the previous config is copied to `.sib-bak` first rather than discarded.

The install places nothing in `$CODEX_HOME/skills/`. Signing is a command the user runs —
`! sib sign "..."` from inside Codex, or the same in their own terminal — and it was never
something an agent could do on their behalf: the ceremony needs their authenticator, and Codex's
sandbox denies the loopback listener it runs on. A skill describing the steps would have been a
how-to that the reviewer correctly treats as untrusted text, and one more thing to keep in step
with the CLI.

Both setup questions need a terminal. Non-interactively, `--yes` takes the suggested context name
and prints it, and a key is never created on a script's behalf — a passkey needs the person at
the authenticator, and a software key is a choice to make deliberately, so the install says how to
enroll one later and leaves the registry empty. With neither a terminal nor `--yes` it refuses
rather than invent a name nobody would see: a wrong audience is not a visible failure, it simply
verifies nothing.

`--audience ID`
: The identifier this harness presents to the verifier, baked into the command the reviewer runs.
  Falls back to `SIB_AUDIENCE` and then the registry's `default_audience`, and asks when none of
  them answers, so you rarely pass it. The installer prints which source it used.

`--config PATH`
: Config file to merge into. The default follows Codex: `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` when that
  variable is set, otherwise `~/.codex/config.toml`. Setting `CODEX_HOME` to a scratch directory
  is the way to try a configuration without touching the real one, since it relocates config,
  auth and state together.

`--sib-path PATH`
: Absolute path to the `sib` binary the reviewer will run (default: the one on `PATH`).

`--home PATH`
: Registry directory, written into the command as `SIB_HOME` (default: `~/.sib`). Keep it outside
  any repository; an agent that can write there can enroll its own key.

`--print`
: Print the configuration and write nothing.

`--yes`
: Answer yes to every question, for scripting. A reviewer you set to another value is still kept.

::: {.callout-note}
The configuration pins Codex's own Guardian prompt template, because `auto_review.extra_policy` is
silently dropped with the template the model catalog serves, which has no `{{ extra_policy }}` slot
(openai/codex#50309). When that is fixed the template pin can go and `extra_policy` alone will do.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
SIB scores authorization, not risk. Codex allows low and medium risk actions whatever the
authorization, so a deploy is only refused when your own policy says that class of action needs
authorizing. Add that rule under `[auto_review]` yourself; the installer says so too.
:::


### allow-authenticator

Add an authenticator model to this registry's `allowed_aaguids`, so its assertions count as
user-verified here. The default list holds models known to verify their user biometrically;
widening it is a policy decision, which is why it is a command rather than a flag on `enroll`.

`AAGUID`
: The AAGUID as `sib enroll` reported it. Case-insensitive. A model already on the default list is
  reported and nothing is written.

`LABEL`
: A name for it, used in the warning messages.

```bash
sib allow-authenticator bada5566-a7aa-401f-bd96-45619a55120d 1Password
```

Think twice before using it for a password manager. With attestation `none` the AAGUID is the
authenticator's own claim, and a vault credential syncs rather than staying on one device, so
"a verified human at this machine" no longer holds.

### audience

Show or set the registry's default audience, which `sign`, `verify` and `install` use when no
audience is given.

`VALUE`
: The authorization context to record. Omit it to print the audience in force and where it came
  from.

```bash
sib audience my-company/trevor-dev     # record it once
sib audience                           # my-company/trevor-dev   (from default_audience in ~/.sib/registry.json)
```

[`sib install codex`](#install-codex) asks for this and records the answer, so recording one by
hand is for renaming a context or scripting an install.

The audience names **one authorization context, not a vendor or a product**: the context within
which signed instructions are valid. A machine is the usual answer, but a bot or a team is as
legitimate — `my-org/slackbot` set on every host running that bot is one context. Matching is
exact: there is no prefix or wildcard logic, so `my-company` does not accept a block signed for
`my-company/trevor-dev`. That is the point — a signature minted for your dev agent must not verify
in CI, in a teammate's checkout, or in anyone else's copy of the same tool. Naming it after the
harness vendor would give every installation in the world the same audience and the check would
stop distinguishing anything.

Both halves must agree, because the signer writes the name into the block and the verifier declares
its own. Three sources are consulted in order, and `sib audience` reports which one won:

1. `--audience` on the command.
2. `SIB_AUDIENCE` in the environment, which is how a test harness overrides one run.
3. `default_audience` in the registry, written by `sib audience` or `sib keygen --audience`.

### verify

Extract and verify every block in a file. Exits with status 0 only when at least one block was
found and every block verified. The mode is enforced once a passkey is enrolled in the registry
and dev before that, unless `SIB_MODE` or a flag says otherwise.

`FILE`
: The file to check, or `-` for standard input.

`--audience ID`
: The audience of this harness; blocks for another audience fail with `audience_mismatch`. Falls
  back to `SIB_AUDIENCE` and then the registry's `default_audience`.

`--enforced`
: Verify in enforced mode: dev-mode blocks and keys confer nothing.

`--dev`
: Verify in dev mode: both kinds of key verify, with the warning.

`--json`
: Print the provenance manifest as JSON instead of the human-readable summary.

### inspect

Decode every block in a file without verifying: the text as written, the clear metadata lines,
the decoded header and the first characters of the signature.

`FILE`
: The file to decode, or `-` for standard input.


## Exit Codes

`sib verify` returns 0 when every block verified, 1 otherwise, including when no block was
found. `sib sign` returns 1 and writes no block when the authenticator's assertion does not
verify, naming the status. The other commands return 0 on success and exit with a message on a
usage error, such as signing with a key that is not enrolled for the signer.


## Environment

`SIB_HOME`
: Directory for dev keys and `registry.json` (default: `~/.sib`).

`SIB_MODE`
: `dev` or `enforced`. It may tighten the default described under `verify` and not loosen it: with
  a passkey enrolled, `SIB_MODE=dev` is reported and ignored, as is any value that is not a mode.
  Use `--dev` for one command. The reason is under
  [What the environment may do](../deep-dives/design-decisions.qmd#what-the-environment-may-do).

`SIB_BROWSER`, `SIB_WEBAUTHN_PORT`, `SIB_REQUIRE_ATTESTATION`, `SIB_ATTESTATION_ROOTS`
: Passkey enrollment and signing; see [Biometric Signing](../components/signing.qmd#environment).
  `SIB_BROWSER` may name an installed browser but not a command to run.
